# The course

## Two courses, one project {.smaller}

**AEM 6991 (fall).** You produce a *plan* — a question, a design, and
evidence that the data exists.

**AEM 6992 (spring).** You *execute* that plan.

The deliverable in December is a proposal somebody could hand to a team in
January.

::: {.notes}
Everything you commit to in the fall you live with in the spring. A
question that is vague in October is a disaster in March.
:::

## What this course is for {.smaller}

By December you should be able to:

- **Find a question** worth a semester, and say why it matters
- **Design** a study that could answer it — and name the assumption
  carrying it
- **Prove the data exists**, can be obtained, and measures what you need
- **Say what you can and cannot claim**, and defend that in a room
- **Work in a team** that delivers on time, with the work split fairly

::: {.notes}
These are the registrar's four outcomes for 6991 plus the two this
section adds — evidence sourcing, and design vocabulary. Do not read
them off. Say the fifth one is graded as hard as the rest, because the
course description calls teamwork a major component and every other
section treats it as goodwill.
:::

## What this is not {.smaller}

You are **not** writing a paper for a journal.

- No gap in the literature to fill
- No contribution to claim
- Nobody is going to referee this for *AJAE*

::: {.notes}
The single most common misunderstanding. Students hear "research design"
and reach for the genre they have seen in seminars. Kill it here.
:::

## What it is {.smaller}

> You are building the analysis a competent team would need before making a
> decision that costs real money.
>
> The standard for "competent" is the same standard a referee would apply.

**Rigor and genre are different axes.** The rigor bar does not move. The
genre does.

::: {.notes}
If the design would not survive a referee, it does not survive here. But
the audience is a decision-maker, not a discipline.

This also rescues the literature review from feeling academic: you read to
find out whether your question is already answered, not to find a gap.
:::

## What good work looks like {.smaller}

The **required headings are the criteria.** If a heading has nothing
under it, that is the finding.

Problem · practical justification · what is already known · conceptual
model · methodological approach · sample · **data and access** ·
internal validity · external validity · **limitations** · work plan ·
ethics · references

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Two questions move a grade more than anything else.

**Is the claim in the first sentence?** And **could it come out the other
way?**
:::

::: {.notes}
This convention is shared across the 6991 sections — criteria are
delivered as the headings a paper must answer, not as a points rubric.
The full quality scale is on the syllabus.

Say the thing they will not expect: stating a limitation well EARNS
marks. Hiding one costs them. Most students arrive believing the
opposite.
:::

## Quizzes {.smaller}

**Short, in class, and without warning.** About six across the semester.

- Three questions, three minutes, on your own device
- **On the lecture you are sitting in**, not on a reading
- Tied to your NetID — it is also the attendance record
- **The lowest is dropped**, so an honest miss costs nothing

::: {.notes}
Say why they are unannounced: a quiz you can revise for is a reading
check, and a quiz you cannot is a reason to be here and paying
attention. That is the thing worth rewarding.

Run item 14 now as the rehearsal — every answer is correct, and it
proves the plumbing before it counts.
:::

## AI: permitted, disclosed, verified {.smaller}

Writing the code is no longer the scarce skill. Neither is drafting the
prose. Knowing what to ask for is. So is noticing when the answer is wrong.

From meeting 12 you work with real data through an assistant. **What is
graded is the questions you ask and the checks you run, never code you
wrote.**

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
McKinsey now runs analyst interviews where you work a problem live on
their AI platform, and they score **how you prompt it, how you catch it
being wrong, and how you turn that into a recommendation.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Say plainly that policies differ across sections and that this one is
deliberately permissive. The McKinsey fact IS the reason, so do not rush
it. Employers put "skills using AI tools" FIRST on what they expect to
value in five years, while ranking it 14th today.

Do NOT bring the grim version into week 1 — entry-level postings down
35%, a third of employers already substituting AI. True, and it will
flatten the room. It belongs in meeting 14.
:::

## The one that will bite you {.smaller}

Ask an assistant for references on your topic. Right now.

Then **open every single one**.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
A fabricated citation in your literature review is an academic integrity
violation.

"The AI generated it" is not a defence. It is an admission that you
submitted something you never read.
:::

::: {.notes}
LIVE DEMO — 5 minutes, do not skip it. Take a topic from the room, ask an
assistant for five references with DOIs, then check them together on the
screen.

Expect a mix: some real, some plausible and wrong — real authors, real
journal, invented title or year. If everything comes back real, say so
honestly and try a narrower topic; the failure rate rises fast as the
topic narrows.

The lesson is not "AI is bad." It is that verification is the one step
you can never delegate, which is the same lesson as meeting 12.
:::

# Finding a question

## Where ideas come from {.smaller}

1. A **gap** in what is known
2. **Extending or contesting** a published result
3. An **anomaly** — something that should not be true
4. A **decision** somebody actually has to make
5. A **dataset** that exists and nobody has looked at properly

Route 5 is the most dangerous, and we come back to why.

::: {.notes}
Routes are where the idea comes from. That is not the same as what shape
it has to take — which is the next twenty minutes, and the part that
actually constrains you.
:::

## This part is the job {.smaller}

Most of your education has rewarded execution. Do the analysis well. Write
it up clearly.

**This course rewards the part before that.** Finding a question worth
answering is a separate skill. It is harder than executing one.

And it is the most enjoyable thing you will do all semester. Do not rush
it.

::: {.notes}
Say this slowly and mean it. Students arrive believing the creative part
is a preamble to the real work. It is the real work — 6992 is where they
execute, and a bad question executed beautifully is still a bad project.
:::

## Is there a method? {.smaller}

Partly. Two ideas have real evidence behind them.

**Start from your means, not your goal.** Experts do not pick a goal and
hunt for means. They start from what they have — who they are, what they
know, whom they know — and work forward.

**Generate, then judge. Never both at once.** Teams that evaluate while
brainstorming produce fewer ideas, and safer ones.

::: {.notes}
The first is effectuation, from Sarasvathy's think-aloud studies of expert
entrepreneurs. It is the licence for what happens this afternoon.

The second is why the relay separates round 1 from the later rounds, and
scores them separately. Say that when you set it up.
:::

## The five archetypes {.smaller}

Every project should be able to say, in one sentence, which of these it is.

| | Archetype | The question |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | **Evaluation** | Did it work? |
| 2 | **Preference & pricing** | What would people choose, and pay? |
| 3 | **Prediction & risk** | What happens next, and how wrong could we be? |
| 4 | **Diagnosis & benchmarking** | Where is the gap, and what explains it? |
| 5 | **Feasibility & landscape** | Is this opportunity real? |

**A project that cannot pick one is not yet a project.**

::: {.notes}
The point of this list is subtraction. "I'm interested in sustainable
packaging" is a topic. Run it through five archetypes and you get five
specific questions — and four you should drop.

The most consistent complaint about capstone courses is that the freedom
is paralyzing. This list is the answer to it.
:::

## 1 · Evaluation {.smaller}

**Did it work?** A decision has already been made somewhere. Estimate its
effect.

- **Claim:** causal, retrospective
- **Design:** difference-in-differences, event study, regression
  discontinuity, IV — *meetings 6–7*
- **Data:** outcomes before and after, for a treated group **and** a
  credible comparison group
- **Fails when:** no comparison group — or the "treatment" was adopted
  precisely by the units already changing

*Did a loyalty-program relaunch change basket size? Did a tariff change
shift import composition?*

::: {.notes}
The single most common failure in the entire course lives on this slide:
selection into treatment. Flag it now, pay it off in meeting 4.
:::

## 2 · Preference & pricing {.smaller}

**What would people choose, and what would they pay?** The decision is not
yet made; the input needed is what people value.

- **Claim:** causal, but about *elicited* choices — a real limitation
- **Design:** choice experiments and conjoint, randomized price or message
  tests — *meetings 6 and 10*
- **Data:** usually collected by you — an instrument you design
- **Fails when:** stated preference reported as revealed preference; or
  n = 40 classmates generalized to a market

*Willingness to pay for a sustainability claim. Which fee structure a
retail investor picks.*

## 3 · Prediction & risk {.smaller}

**What happens next, and how wrong could we be?** The decision needs a
number about the future, not a cause.

- **Claim:** predictive — **explicitly not causal**, and saying so is part
  of the grade
- **Design:** out-of-sample validation, backtesting, honest baselines
- **Data:** panel or time series with enough history to hold out a test
  period
- **Fails when:** no out-of-sample test; look-ahead bias; or the team
  quietly starts making causal recommendations off a predictive model

*Default risk. Demand forecasting. Churn.*

::: {.notes}
40% of this class goes into finance, where this is often the honest
project. I am not banning it. The discipline is naming it: "this is
predictive, here is why that is right for this decision, here is what I
therefore cannot conclude." That sentence is the whole course.
:::

## 4 · Diagnosis & benchmarking {.smaller}

**Where is the gap, and what explains it?** Something varies more than it
should and nobody knows why.

- **Claim:** descriptive, hypothesis-generating
- **Design:** decomposition, benchmarking against a reference group —
  *meetings 9 and 12*
- **Data:** operational or administrative records at the unit where the
  variation lives
- **Fails when:** description dressed up as a cause; or it stops at "here
  is a dashboard" with no decision attached

*Why conversion differs threefold across regions. Where a hiring funnel
leaks.*

## 5 · Feasibility & landscape {.smaller}

**Is this opportunity real, and what constrains it?**

- **Claim:** descriptive synthesis, **plus at least one original empirical
  component**
- **Design:** market sizing, competitive benchmarking, regulatory and cost
  constraints
- **Fails when:** it becomes a deck of secondary research

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The dangerous one.** Approved only if it contains a specific, checkable
empirical question you answer with data you analyze yourselves.
:::

::: {.notes}
The type most likely to produce a bad capstone, and the one
consulting-bound students gravitate to. The guardrail is real and it gets
enforced at the outline's data section, which is due at meeting 12.
:::

## What the last two cohorts did {.smaller}

**2026**

ESG strategy → return on equity · inventory turnover → performance ·
investor sentiment → S&P return · Wikipedia pageviews → stock returns ·
what drives engagement on TikTok

**2023**

Twitter sentiment → NFT returns · social media sentiment → stock return ·
weather → stock return · ESG score → annual return · organic food choices ·
sustainability and Gen Z purchasing

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Four of the five 2026 projects are the same project.** What is it?
:::

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Do not answer it for them — someone will get there, and it
lands infinitely harder from a student than from me.

The answer: take a public signal anybody can download, regress a financial
outcome on it, report a coefficient. Free data, no design, no decision
attached.

Then the question that matters: WHY did that happen? Not laziness. The
data was free and available and the question got shaped to fit it. That is
anti-pattern 2, and it is the default unless you actively resist it.

Then the permission they need to hear: the most ambitious project anyone
remembers ran online experiments on brand recognition, then talked a soda
company into donating thousands of cans and ran a field experiment in
dining halls. Nine-month MPS team. No econometrics — nerve, and knowing it
was allowed. It is allowed.
:::

## Six anti-patterns {.smaller}

1. **The topic with no question.** "AI in finance."
2. **The dataset in search of a question.** You found a nice dataset and
   have been reverse-engineering a question onto it since.
3. **The consulting deck.** Archetype 5 without the empirical component.
4. **The unobtainable-data project.** Beautiful design; requires
   proprietary data from a firm nobody on the team knows.
5. **The dissertation.** Correctly scoped for three years.
6. **The already-answered question.** This is what the literature review
   is *for*.

::: {.notes}
Number 2 is why this course is ordered question, then design, then data.
Teams who find data first rationalize a question around it, every time.

Number 4 has to die by meeting 12, in the outline's data section. Not in
January.
:::

## The feasibility filter {.smaller}

Four questions. A "no" on any one is fatal — and cheap to discover *now*.

1. Could a team of 3–5 execute this in **one spring semester**?
2. Can you name the **specific dataset**, who holds it, and how you get it
   — *checked, not assumed*?
3. Does the design produce an answer that **could come out either way**?
4. Would somebody **actually act differently** depending on the answer?

::: {.notes}
Question 2 is the one they will fudge. Push on "checked, not assumed" —
have you opened the page, found the access terms, seen the actual columns?

This filter is what session B runs on. Do not cut it.
:::

# Session B · The literature

## Why you search {.smaller}

Not to find a gap. To answer two questions:

1. **Has somebody already answered this?** If yes, that is good news found
   cheaply — change the question now, not in November.
2. **How do people answer questions like this?** The design, the data
   source, the unit of analysis. You are shopping for a method.

::: {.notes}
Frame it as reconnaissance, not scholarship. That reframing is what makes
it tolerable for students who did not come here to read journals.
:::

## How to search {.smaller}

- **Start broad, then chase citations.** One good recent paper gives you
  its reference list *and* everything that has cited it since.
- **Google Scholar, then the library.** Cornell has access to nearly
  everything; use the library proxy rather than paying anyone.
- **Read in this order:** abstract → figures and tables → conclusion →
  method. Most papers are decided in the first three.
- **Business sources count.** Industry reports, trade press, company
  filings. For most of your archetypes these matter more than journals.

## How to screen {.smaller}

For each candidate, one line:

| Question | Design | Data | What they found | Why it matters to us |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|

Five to eight rows is a literature review at this stage. Eighty is
procrastination.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Every reference gets opened.** Not the abstract someone quoted at you.
The paper.
:::

## What you already have {.smaller}

Before you assume data has to be bought, found, or scraped:

- **The Cornell library's licensed holdings.** Far more than most
  students realise, and already paid for.
- **Dewey** — a commercial data marketplace Cornell JCB subscribes to.
  **You have access at no cost.**

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Teams routinely propose buying data the College already has. Others
abandon a good question because they assumed the data was out of reach.
Check first.
:::

**Register tonight** at [app.deweydata.io](https://app.deweydata.io) with
your **Cornell email** — approval is a human step, so you will not have
access this minute.

Worked examples of getting from a dataset to a question:
[**Project ideas**](../project-ideas.qmd)

::: {.notes}
Browse Dewey live on the projector — from YOUR account. Students will
not have access yet: registration needs a Cornell email and then a manual
approval by an institutional admin, which takes days. So today is a
demonstration, not a hands-on. Tell them to register tonight so they are
approved in time for the feasibility work.

Confirm the login works on the room machine before class.

The point is filter question 2, from session A: "can you name the
specific dataset, who holds it, and how you get it — checked, not
assumed." For a lot of questions the honest answer changes once you
know what you already have.
:::

## Working backwards from a dataset {.smaller}

Pick one nobody in the room chose. Then:

1. What could this data **answer**?
2. Which of those would anybody **act on**?
3. What does it **not** contain that you would need?

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
This is route 5 done properly. Route 5 done badly is anti-pattern 2 —
finding a dataset and rationalising a question onto it. The difference
is that here the question still has to survive the filter, and you are
allowed to walk away from the data.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do this live, as a room. Five or six minutes, after the Dewey browse.
It is a demonstration of the move, not the exercise itself — the relay
is the exercise.

The tension is real and worth naming out loud: I spent session A saying
design before data, and now I am showing you a data catalogue in the
first meeting. The resolution is that knowing what you can get changes
which questions are *feasible* — it does not change what makes a
question good. You still start from the question. You just stop
proposing ones whose data you will never hold.

Note the symmetry with how we will do writing later in the term: take
the finished artifact apart to see the structure underneath, then build
your own the same way. Reverse-engineering is a method here, not a
trick.
:::

## The question relay {.smaller}

Groups of four. Points.

**Your group holds one dataset card.** After each round, **the datasets
move one way and the question sheets move the other** — so no group ever
gets its own question back.

| The move | You get | You do |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Write** | A dataset | Write the best question it could answer |
| **Break & build** | A new dataset **+** somebody's question | **Break their question**, then write your own |
| **Break & combine** | A new dataset **+** somebody's question | Break it, then **combine** any two datasets you have held |

[Dataset cards and question sheet →](../handouts/relay-cards.qmd)

::: {.notes}
Groups of four. With ~25 in the room that is six or seven groups, and
nine cards are printed, so you have spares.

DECIDE TWO ROUNDS OR THREE NOW, and announce it. Two rounds is Write,
then Break & combine — 14 minutes each, leaving a full 12 for read-outs.
Three rounds is 10, 11 and 11, and read-outs drop to 6. Two is the
recommendation for week 1, when you do not yet know how fast this room
works.

Say out loud that this grouping is TEMPORARY — real teams form from the
statements of interest before meeting 2. Otherwise some of them will
spend the hour negotiating instead of working.

Cards: the nine datasets on the project-ideas page, printed. Pass
datasets clockwise and sheets anticlockwise, so nobody ever breaks their
own question.
:::

## Scoring {.smaller}

- **+1** every time a question of yours **survives** a break attempt
- **+1** every break you **land** — you must name *which* filter kills it
- **+2** for the best **combination** question, decided by the room

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
"I don't like it" is not a break. Name the filter:
**scope** · **data you can actually get** · **could come out either way**
· **somebody would act on it**
:::

::: {.notes}
The scoring is doing real work, so do not soften it. Points for breaking
teach the filter faster than points for building — and it rehearses the
referee report they write in December.

The combination bonus is the real prize. Dewey's datasets join on
lat/long, ZIP, brand, company and ticker, so the good questions live in
the joins. Say so before the combination round starts, not after.
:::

## Round 1 · write {.smaller}

**What could this data answer?**

Write three candidates. Then pick your best, put it at the top of the
sheet, and label its **archetype**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
You did not choose this dataset. That is the point — it is the same move
you make when somebody hands you a business problem you did not pick.
:::

::: {.notes}
Circulate. Two failure modes to catch early: questions that are still
topics ("housing affordability"), and questions the dataset cannot
actually speak to.

Call the last two minutes out loud, then rotate firmly. The clock is
part of the exercise, so do not let a group talk past it.
:::

## Then break, and build {.smaller}

**First, break the question you inherited.** Four filters. Write which
one kills it — or write *survives*, honestly.

**Then build.** On your new dataset — or, in the combination round, on
**any two datasets your group has held**.

::: {.notes}
Give the break half about six minutes of whatever the round is, then
call time and move them to building.

In the combination round, walk the room saying the join keys out loud —
parcels and stores and chargers all carry lat/long; postings and layoffs
carry company; scanner and card data carry brand. That hint is what
turns the combination from harder into better.

Watch for the group that breaks everything on filter 2 because "we
can't get the data." Push: you have the dataset in your hand. Filter 2
is about *this* data, not imaginary data.
:::

## Read-outs {.smaller}

**The two best combination questions.** And **one good kill** — the
question, and which filter did it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A question you kill in August is a month you do not lose in March.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes. Do the kill LAST and dwell on it — the killing is the
lesson, not the winner.

If nothing got killed all afternoon, say so plainly: it means the filter
was applied too gently, and promise to push harder next week.

Collect every sheet. They are the artifact, and they tell you who in
this room already thinks like this.
:::

## Before next week {.smaller}

**Statement of interest** — one to two pages, due before meeting 2.

- What you might want to work on, and why it matters
- What you want out of it professionally
- **Which archetype**, and why

**I form the teams from these.** Meeting 2 is causal language, and your
team writes down its own ground rules.

::: {.notes}
Say explicitly: not being able to pick an archetype is useful information,
not a failure. It means the idea is still a topic. Write that down and I
will help.
:::

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

### The arc

AEM 6991 produces a *plan*; AEM 6992 *executes* it. The deliverable in
December is a proposal somebody could hand to a team in January.

### AI ground rules

Permitted by default, disclosure mandatory, verification graded. From
meeting 12 you work with real data through an assistant, and what is
graded is the questions you ask and the checks you run — never code you
wrote.

**Every reference gets opened.** A fabricated citation is an academic
integrity violation, and "the AI generated it" is an admission that you
submitted something you never read.

### What this is, and is not

You are not writing a paper for a journal — there is no gap to fill and no
contribution to claim. You are building the analysis a competent team would
need before making a decision that costs real money, and the standard for
"competent" is the same standard a referee would apply. Rigor and genre are
different axes: the rigor bar does not move, the genre does.

This is also why the literature matters without the project being a
literature project. You read to find out whether your question is already
answered, and how people have answered questions like it.

For context, MPS AEM class of 2025: 40% into finance, 21% marketing and
sales, 15% general management, 13% consulting, 6% data and analytics.
Essentially none into research.

### Where ideas come from

Five routes: a gap in what is known; extending or contesting a published
result; an anomaly; a decision somebody has to make; a dataset nobody has
looked at properly. The last is the most dangerous.

### Coming up with the idea is the job

Most of your education has rewarded execution. This course rewards the
part before it. A bad question executed beautifully is still a bad
project.

It is also the most enjoyable part of the work. Give it the time.

### Is there a method for having ideas?

Partly. Two of the popular answers have real evidence; most do not.

**Start from your means, not your goal.** This is
[effectuation](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2001.4378020), from Saras Sarasvathy's think-aloud
studies of expert entrepreneurs. Experts do not pick a goal and search
for the means to reach it. They start from who they are, what they know
and whom they know, and work forward. Sarasvathy's phrase is that they
*make* opportunities rather than find them.

You have a Dewey account, a concentration and a team with particular
backgrounds. Working forward from those is not a lesser way of doing it.
It is what expertise looks like. What keeps it honest is the feasibility
filter — means-driven reasoning turns into anti-pattern 2 the moment you
stop being willing to walk away from the means.

**Generate, then judge. Never both at once.** Teams that evaluate while
brainstorming produce fewer ideas, and safer ones. The relay separates
the two on purpose, and scores them separately.

**Ask what job somebody is hiring the answer to do.**
[Jobs to be Done](https://hbr.org/2016/09/know-your-customers-jobs-to-be-done) reframes a question from "what does
this do" to "what is somebody trying to accomplish". That is feasibility
filter 4, arrived at from another direction. The reframing is useful; the
evidence behind it is thin.

**For research questions specifically**,
[Sandberg and Alvesson](https://doi.org/10.1177/1350508410372151) separate *gap-spotting* — finding
what the literature has not covered — from *problematization*, which
challenges an assumption the literature shares. Gap-spotting is easier
and produces most published work. Problematization produces the
interesting work and is riskier. For one semester, gap-spotting is
usually right. Knowing which you are doing is what stops you overclaiming.

A caution that applies here as everywhere in this course. **Being taught
in every business school is not evidence that something works.** Design
thinking as a branded five-step method, and lean startup, are widely
taught and lightly tested.

### The five archetypes

Every project should be able to say in one sentence which of these it is. A
project that cannot pick one is not yet a project.

| | Archetype | Question | Claim | Design | Fails when |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Evaluation | Did it work? | Causal, retrospective | DiD, event study, RD, IV | No credible comparison group |
| 2 | Preference & pricing | What would they choose and pay? | Causal, but elicited | Choice experiments, conjoint | Stated read as revealed |
| 3 | Prediction & risk | What happens next? | Predictive, *not causal* | Out-of-sample validation | Causal claims off a predictive model |
| 4 | Diagnosis & benchmarking | Where is the gap? | Descriptive | Decomposition, benchmarking | Description dressed as cause |
| 5 | Feasibility & landscape | Is this real? | Synthesis + original work | Market sizing, benchmarking | No empirical component |

Archetype 5 is approved only if it contains a specific, checkable empirical
question you answer with data you analyze yourselves.

### Six anti-patterns

The topic with no question; the dataset in search of a question; the
consulting deck; the unobtainable-data project; the dissertation; the
already-answered question.

### The feasibility filter

1. Could a team of 3–5 execute this in one spring semester?
2. Can you name the specific dataset, who holds it, and how you get it —
   checked, not assumed?
3. Does the design produce an answer that could come out either way?
4. Would somebody actually act differently depending on the answer?

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

### The literature workshop

You search for two reasons: to find out whether somebody has already
answered your question, and to see how people answer questions like it.

Start broad, then chase citations — one good recent paper gives you its
reference list and everything citing it since. Read abstract, then figures
and tables, then conclusion, then method. Business sources count; for most
archetypes they matter more than journals.

Screen with one line per paper: question, design, data, what they found,
why it matters to us. Five to eight rows is enough at this stage.

### What you already have access to

Before assuming data must be bought or scraped: the Cornell library's
licensed holdings, and **Dewey**, a commercial data marketplace the Johnson
College of Business subscribes to and which you can use at no cost. Teams
routinely propose buying data the College already has, or drop a good
question because they assumed the data was unreachable.

**Register at [app.deweydata.io](https://app.deweydata.io) with your
Cornell email**, in week 1. Your account sits pending until an
administrator approves it, so do not leave it until you need the data.

If you are stuck, there is a numbered list of leads under Resources —
[potential project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd). Treat it as a way to
get unstuck, not a menu. Nobody has ever written a good capstone from
somebody else's idea list.

Working backwards from a dataset is legitimate — it is route 5 — provided
you do it honestly: what could this answer, which of those would anybody act
on, and what does it not contain that you would need? The question still has
to survive the filter, and you are still allowed to walk away from the data.
Route 5 done badly is anti-pattern 2.

### The question relay

Groups of four. Between rounds the datasets move one way and the question
sheets move the other, so no group ever gets its own question back. Three
moves, run over two or three rounds depending on the clock.

**Write.** You are handed a dataset you did not choose. What could it
answer? Write three candidates, pick your best, label its archetype.

**Break, then build.** You get a new dataset *and* somebody else's
question. Break their question first — name which of the four filters
kills it, or record honestly that it survives. Then write your own on the
new dataset.

**Break, then combine.** Break again, then build the best question you can
from **any two datasets your group has held**. Dewey's datasets join on
latitude and longitude, ZIP, brand, company and ticker, and the good
questions usually live in those joins.

**Scoring.** One point each time a question of yours survives a break, one
point for every break you land, two points for the best combination
question. "I don't like it" is not a break — you have to name the filter.

The nine dataset cards and the question sheet are a
[printable handout](../handouts/relay-cards.qmd); the same nine, with what
each joins on, are also listed on the
[project ideas](../project-ideas.qmd) page. Cross out the failures and name
which filter killed them.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.
